newsitem.title: UK: MGAM given symbolic fine, but reputation tarnished.
newsitem.headline: MGAM given symbolic fine, but reputation tarnished.

text.p: A record fine slapped on Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) on Wednesday was likely to raise unwanted publicity for the firm but was unlikely to have a further material effect on business, industry sources said.
"Today's news is really only symbolic," said a fund analyst who asked not to be named.
Britain's investment watchdogs announced a record two million pound ($3.3 million) fine on the fund management arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank for a catalogue of rule breaches and management failings.
The Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) also imposed costs of a million pounds on two MGAM units and said they had not informed it about management problems.

IMRO added that at least one MGAM board member knew of problems at the funds, two of which were managed by Peter Young, by April 1996. The funds were not suspended until last September when serious irregularities in valuations of unlisted securities were discovered.

The analyst said the fine was small relative to the size of the group and the cost of the scandal so far. "The IMRO fines are going to have to get bigger if they are to have any effect. I feel it is a record that is unlikely to last very long."
IMRO Chief Executive Phillip Thorpe said the mismanagement of the funds had "caused unnecessary concern to an enormous number of investors".
The suspended funds included the Morgan Grenfell European Growth Trust, the Morgan Grenfell Europa Fund and the Dublin-based Morgan Grenfell European Capital Growth Fund.
The industry analyst said the knock for the group would come from the renewed publicity over the scandal, and its possible effect on new business.
"They will be fighting in the market for new business, but as it happens they have some other very good funds in their stable," an industry source said.

Soon after the three funds resumed trading in September last year, MGAM said it lost in outflows some 256 million pounds. The industry source said MGAM had not lost a lot more than that in the following weeks.

The unit trust industry itself suffered initially as a result of the affair. In September net retail sales fell to 224 million pounds from nearly 400 million the month before. Since then they have recovered, with February inflows of 483 million recorded.
In the European unit trust sector, outflows of 115 million pounds were recorded in September, but inflows of between 26 and 56 million sterling have been registered since.
"It is a severe and salutary lesson to the unit trust industry and we hope it never happens again," Association of Unit Trusts and Investment Funds (AUTIF) director general Philip Warland said.
But he commended the speed of restitution to investors.
"I don't think I can think of any other problem in the financial world where the underlying clients have not only got their money back but got restitution and more."
He said the effect of the MGAM affair on the industry as a whole had been limited.
"It is a shifting of business. Last September they did indeed dip but within a month they were back on trend and certainly if you speak to Independent Financial Advisers (IFAs) that is what happened.
"If they advised their clients that they should be in a European fund what they tended to do is transfer to another European fund," said Warland.

John Conroy, European head of asset consulting at pension fund consultant Towers Perrin, said the IMRO investigation would resurrect the issue temporarily, but doubted whether it would be a differentiating factor in clients' decisions on where to put their funds.
"It may bring it back into the public domain for a little while but I don't think it will be a deciding factor."

He said clients on balance had remained with MGAM through the scandal and the later publicity surrounding fund manager Nicola Horlick. MGAM suspended Horlick in January, accusing her of negotiating to defect to a rival bank with a team of colleagues.
